messages.author: 98eff7f1d92b1b85
messages.subject: Errors on latent variables
parts:
Hopefully this question has not been answered many times before. I had a hard time finding the answer at least, and would be really happy with any help.

I have a model with exogenous and endogenous observed variables ("exo" and "endo"), and several latent variables ("latent"). My real model contains a lot of these variables, but I have made a toy example, shown below. The exogenous variables predict the latent variables, and the latent variables are manifested by the endogenous variables.

The toy model is:
"latent1 =~ gamma1_1*endo1
latent1 =~ gamma1_2*endo2
latent2 =~ gamma2_3*endo3
latent1 ~ alpha1_1*exo1
latent1 ~ alpha1_2*exo2
latent1 ~ alpha1_3*exo3
latent2 ~ alpha2_1*exo1
latent2 ~ alpha2_2*exo2
latent2 ~ alpha2_3*exo3
latent1 ~~ latent_covar1_2*latent2
latent_covar1_2 == 0
latent1 ~~ 1*latent1
latent2 ~~ 1*latent2
endo1 ~~ endo_var*endo1
endo2 ~~ endo_var*endo2
endo3 ~~ endo_var*endo3
1 == gamma1_1^2 + gamma1_2^2
1 == gamma2_3^2"

I used "std.lv=T" in fitting it (and then manually confirmed it with "latent1 ~~ 1*latent1"), since I already have restrictions on the factor loadings. If I leave out the exogenous variables, I can reproduce the results of a PCA (up to rotation). I have also run the model with free error variances on the endogenous variables, which would make it more like a factor analysis.

My question is: what do the errors on the latent variables ("latent1 ~~ x*latent1") mean in this case? In a model without the exogenous observed variables, I would interpret this as the variance of the latent variable. However, in this case, would it be the errors on the linear models for the latent variables (like "latent1 =~ gamma1_1*endo1")? Wouldn't it then make more sense to leave them to be estimated freely, as enforced by ("latent1 ~~ NA*latent1")? This seems to hinder identification (alpha estimates blow up). Any advice?

Thank you for your help!
Sjoerd

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Errors on latent variables
parts:
My question is: what do the errors on the latent variables ("latent1 ~~ x*latent1") mean in this case? ... would it be the errors on the linear models for the latent variables (like "latent1 =~ gamma1_1*endo1")?

Yes, you answered your own question.
Wouldn't it then make more sense to leave them to be estimated freely, as enforced by ("latent1 ~~ NA*latent1")?

The latent (residual or total) variance is not identified because you haven't measured it (only its indicators).  So you have to "give it a scale" by either fixing its (residual or total) variance to 1 or by fixing a factor loading to 1 (std.lv = FALSE). The choice is arbitrary because the two choices lead to statistically equivalent models, and the standardized solutions will be identical (although SEs for model parameters are not proportionally equivalent, in general).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I understand fixing a parameter is needed in a latent variable model. However, I think I have already fixed the scale of my latent variables by using "1 == gamma1_1^2 + gamma1_2^2" and "1 == gamma2_3^2". Isn't this a suitable alternative to fixing the latent variable variance or one of the loadings? In fact, for the second latent variable I do actually fix the (only) loading to 1 (or -1). My problem lies in the fact that my latent variables are also predicted by exogenous variables, and I would think that this part of the model does not need any scale-fixation, since this is already taken care of by fixing the sum of squared loadings of the endogenous variables. However, I do not seem to get a sensible estimation when I free up the latent variable variance (by overriding "std.lv=T" with "latent1 ~~ NA*latent1" and "latent2 ~~ NA*latent2").
